utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I did not. I -- the bodies were sent down to the pathology and anthropology team that were in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. The other issue I wanted to ask you about is, there is also, is there not, in forensic anthropology, a practice or a formula known as -- whereby you estimate the minimum number of people in a -- in a grave?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Minimum number of individuals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, tell me, how does that work? How does that process work? And obviously bearing in mind that we are not anthropologists here, can you explain it in very simple terms?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, very simply what you would do is you would take single bones and you would count to see which ones are repeated the most. For example --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just -- can I stop you there. When you say "single bones," do you engage in a process of determining bones from the left-hand side of the body or the right-hand side of the body or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, you would not only determine side but you might determine -- you might want to subdivide that into thirds, for example, the proximal third of a left humerus in comparison to a mid-third of a right humerus, for example. So you would then basically count to see which bone or fragment of bone appears the most amount of times, to determine the minimum number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And here, did you engage in that process yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, once again, this is not something you would do in a field environment, this is something you would do in a morgue. So we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to -- and obviously you've been asked about your role at Lazete 2, but you also were involved in the year 2000 at the site at Ravnice, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Initially, yeah. I was there at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, what time of the year were you there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: This was after Lazete 2 and while we were beginning to look for the graves at Glogova, if I can recall correctly, it was -- it must have been mid-August, the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you, no doubt, took notes and the like when you were at -- performing your tasks at Ravnice?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And did you ever produce a report in relation to your findings at that site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I did not. That site was cancelled, if I'm not mistaken when the transition was made between myself and Professor Richard Wright.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, just so that we clarify this, you are not suggesting that Richard Wright was, in fact, responsible for Ravnice after you, are you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, in fact, yes. Since I was his deputy, when he came back, he was a senior forensic archaeologist on site. In reality, the report similar in the case, as in the case of Lazete 2, was never requested, and I was told later that that site was finished or handed over to -- to the Bosnian commission, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, and just when you say that -- and we'll take this step by step. You say that with Lazete 2 a report was never requested. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: It was requested initially, and then it was never requested after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, initially, who made the request?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Dean Manning, if I'm not mistaken, an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: An investigator.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And he withdrew that request, this is in relation to Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. He then received the Lazete 1 report and they were very happy with it and we never spoke it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But we make sure did -- when you say he then received the Lazete 1 report, do you mean your Lazete 1 report or Bill Haglund's Lazete 1 report? Because there is obviously going to be some confusion here?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Bill Haglund only worked at Lazete 2. I was the only one who worked at Lazete 1 and then also worked at Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, in relation to Ravnice, again, was it Dean Manning who made the initial request for the report from you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't recall, but it must have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to take you first of all just to some aspects of his report on Ravnice, okay? This is Dean Manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, if the witness could be shown P648. And if we go to page 9 of that document. That's page 9 in English, hopefully the B/C/S will be the same. Do you want me to -- P648. Okay. You have that up there at the left of your screen, Mr. Peccerelli. You see the heading there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just before I do take you to his report, would you agree with me if I suggested to you that it would be quite inaccurate to describe Ravnice as a grave?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I would. It was not a grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not a grave at all, it was -- it's more correct, isn't it, to say that it was simply bodies found on an embankment, on a steep slope?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: It would be surface find of human remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Most likely a dump site.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. So if we then go to what Mr. Manning's comments about this -- this grave, it's -- can we take it that whatever anthropological or archaeological information that is in Dean Manning's report, he has gleaned that from you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If he was at the site, he could -- because of his experience, he could probably come up with some of these explanations himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But he's a policeman?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. He has no --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Investigator.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- anthropological or archaeological training himself?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So can I ask you this: When you were present at Ravnice, was Dean Manning there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. And there is no other archaeological -- there is no other anthropologist or archaeologists that were responsible for Ravnice in this period in 2000 that we're talking about, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. Richard Wright.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to what you say about Richard Wright's involvement here. Just insofar as what you know when you were there, you were the lead archaeologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: While I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now, I want to particularly take you to what Dean Manning says at the -- in the first paragraph. The second last line he makes the observation, "Bodies were caught up in trees and a fence along the middle of the slope." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. Can you perhaps tell me a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't recall a fence. I do have a recall of trees and as the bodies were rolling down the slope, some of them got caught up in some trees.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And he then went on to make the observation underneath the heading "aerial imagery" on the second line, "It is believed that this site is connected with the Srebrenica deaths; however, further examination of the site is necessary." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, before you arrived at this site were you told by Dean Manning that it was believed that the remains at this site were persons executed in relation to Srebrenica? Is that what you were informed?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I was told that those bodies might belong to people that were killed inside of a warehouse, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So you were given specific information about people being -- having met their death in that manner. But when Dean Manning makes that observation that further examination of the site was necessary in order to confirm what was originally thought, is that as a result of any observations you made about the state of the remains?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the remains were skeletonised, and I think the proper thing would have been to recover all the remains while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But that wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Not while I was there. I was -- Professor Richard Wright returned and -- when I left. I found out later that the site was stopped, and as I told you earlier, handed over to the Bosnian commission, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, were you ever, in the context of your professional capacity at Ravnice, were you ever asked to provide an opinion to Dean Manning about how you considered these persons to have met their death?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. Was there anything about the observations you made at the site that caused you to consider that those skeletal remains were there as a result of conflict or a combat situation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I couldn't tell either. What we -- what we found were human skeletal remains dumped on a slope on -- off a dirt track. It's not something you expect to find, but I couldn't say whether it was combat related or any -- otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And if, as you know, this was circumstances where there were no blindfolds located on the bodies, were there? I'm reading from Dean Manning's report, so --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the report, if you have a look --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If that's what it says, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You accept that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That no ligatures were located either?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That's what it says, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. So in those circumstances, if that scenario was put to you in terms of these people having met their death in a conflict or combat situation, you certainly couldn't exclude that, could you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: As a possible?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I couldn't exclude either.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I couldn't exclude either, whether it was combat or just a conflict situation. I mean it's -- you cannot just say that because the bodies didn't have blindfolds or ligatures that they were one thing or the other. I mean, either way, those bodies -- those bodies, they died somehow. We would have to look into it further, not only in the recovery aspect of it's about but also in the morgue before being able to make a determination, a more educated determination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Can I ask you this then: Is it -- that observation that Dean Manning makes, where he says that it's believed that the site's connected to Srebrenica, but further examination it necessary, does that accord with your observations of the site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, my observations of the site, that site or any other site, were not to the extent of trying to link the bodies to a specific event. I think in the sense that Dean Manning is speaking, he is speaking as an investigator, and in that sense he had all the information about trying to link all these different graves to possible events. In my experience in working in Bosnia, I was always asked to recover, find the graves, recover the bodies, and document the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to work backwards. Move away from Ravnice. And in particular, I want to ask you about Lazete 1. Is it possible, from an anthropological point of view, to date graves, or grave sites? Is that -- you understand what my question is?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Archaeologically, yes, there are methods to date organic components within the grave. What is usually done in more recent graves is you look at the context of the grave, for example, coins, maybe newspapers or any publications with the date on them, and from there you might make an estimation of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you're -- what you say is from inference, from the process of drawing inferences from material found in the grave. That's one thing that you're talking about. Because Professor Wright's already given evidence here, and I just want to ask if you agree with what he said, which was: He said it's technically not possible to date graves using the ordinary methods available to archaeology. That was his evidence.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, like I mentioned, if you can -- if you find artefacts within the context, it is a viable method. I do understand that it is not something that is used ordinarily in these types of graves but if you want an estimate, you can do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But to be exact, it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, your assessment of Lazete 1 was that it was a primary disturbed grave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, what are the indications of whether or not a grave can be considered a secondary grave? What do you usually look for?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In a secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, we look for most of its contents to be non-articulated human remains. Usually --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: By that you mean, sorry, disjointed bodies parts?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, basically disjointed body parts, many, many loose bones.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Umm --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about, sorry, can I suggest something to you?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about foreign -- what about soil that's foreign to the area in which you are conducting the exhumation, is that an indication, or could be an indication?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Of course. If you find foreign soil that isn't natural to a specific area, it might be inferred as well that it was transported there from someplace else, along with the contents of -- or the fill that was within the primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So if I could take you, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is P02459, Your Honour, at page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is your first report for Lazete 1. And page 15. That's it. Now, I think there's two English versions there. Okay. If I can just direct your attention to the final paragraph of that -- of your report. If you can just have a read of that to yourself. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, that first observation that you make there is in relation to the quality of the soil, and you do make the observation that it's possibly foreign soil introduced to the area of Lazete 1?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No? That's not what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, no, no. What the difference is, is that in the primary grave, the soil had been compacting and -- under the same conditions for the same amount of time. During this -- in the other parts of the grave, the soil was taken out and most likely mixed again with topsoil before it was filled again. So that difference in time period and the difference in the consistency of the soil can be seen because it was removed, not that it was introduced from someplace else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not that it was foreign --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- and introduced?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I literally have one or two more questions and then I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You then go on to make observations about the robbing areas and you then make an estimation. Do you see that in the further part of the paragraph? You say, "If 127 bodies were exhumed from approximately 65 per cent of the grave, I estimate that a potential 68 bodies could have been removed during LZ01." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, how do you make an estimate like that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You would take the amount of area and volume that the other bodies occupy within the grave and then calculate if the same was to be true in those two areas. Then that would hold true.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If the same wasn't, then it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So it's fair to say, is it not, that that conclusion that you draw there is just an entire -- it's entirely as a result of presumption on your part?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You have to make presumptions in order to do it?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And just so that I am -- clarify with you, that number of 68 bodies, that didn't eventually find its way into any numerical estimation that you gave to an investigator?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I never spoke to an investigator after I presented the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But just so that -- so whenever you provided numbers of -- of bodies that were recovered in your report, of Lazete 1, that's the only one that I've asked you about, the 127 bodies that you speak of, they were complete bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We counted them as bodies. Some of them were truncated bodies, and there were also body parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, is the 127 bodies, is that the result of a minimum number of persons calculation, or is it simply what -- the calculation you made as a result of your involvement at the site? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The 127 number is the number of body sheets that were filled within the grave. In other words, if a body was more than half complete we assigned it a body number. It didn't have to be a complete body to be given a body number. On the other hand, if there was loose bones that might be able to give us information for identification purposes then those would be handed body part numbers, but in no way is that an inference of a minimum number of individuals in that grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. -- is it Peccerelli or Pecerelli?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me if I mispronounce it. First off, I just want to ask you about the fact that you have testified that in the last 12 years of's work in the recovery, exhumation, as a forensic anthropologist in Guatemala and elsewhere. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you have -- you have done a lot of work in those years on digs that concern humanitarian issues. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then you've also done digs such as for the -- this Tribunal, which involve not only humanitarian issues but possibly criminal investigations, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: All the -- the graves that we investigated in Guatemala are also for criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And in your field as a forensic anthropologist dealing with these types of exhumations and recoveries, who do you believe to be the highest expert in this field in the world?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Personally who do I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, I've been fortunate to have had teachings of Dr. Clyde Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I want to ask you a question, if I might, in regards to the dating of graves themselves. I think that you testified just recently that you believe that from an anthropological point of view, you -- it is possible to date a grave site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, contextually within archaeology, if something is placed stratographically within a grave and you find it associated to some other find within the grave you can tell something about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. And doctor, I don't want to try to jump around, but I'm going to have to, I've been asked to try to finish you up so you can fly elsewhere tomorrow morning. I'm going to talk a minute about what you call Lazete 2 site.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And as you may or may not know, we've just been given information about that very recently by the Office of the Prosecutor. But in any event, on page 16 of your report you state there were -- and please go ahead and get that, if you'd like, find that.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You say that -- I believe this is a conclusion that there were "four excavations that were detected at site Lazete 2, including current ICTY investigation: 1. You have put down original grave (between July 5th and July 27th, 1995)". Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, please, how you came up with the beginning date of July 5th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: From an aerial image that I was given, where I think it is on page -- let me find it. 11. There's also an -- it's also clearer in the Lazete 1 report. It's the same image, because these two sites are so close to each other. I was given these images with these dates showing no disturbance on July 5th and then showing two clear disturbances on the sites where we located the graves on July 27. I thereby infer that between those dates is when those disturbances occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor, you just stated that the July 5th was an aerial image showing no disturbed earth, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then you said showing two clear disturbances on the site where we located the graves on July 27th. Maybe I misunderstood, but you didn't locate the grave on July 27th, but --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, we located the grave later in 2000, but that date of the picture is July 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, to be -- so two questions. First off, the reason that you would have put that down would have been information given to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, correct? The aerial images?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I was given these images, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: By the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: By the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Second off, how many other aerial images were you shown besides the two that you have put down on page 11?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The other ones are the ones in the Lazete 1 report. It may be the same ones, if you allow me to look at that. On page 11 of the Lazete 1 report. There's two more images of Lazete 1, and these four images are the four images I was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, by the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You indicated that your first trip to Bosnia was in 1997; is that correct? For Brcko?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Brcko, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you mentioned that, a number of different people from different countries, who from the United States was along with you that you can recall on that site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Klirkoff [phoen] if I don't -- mistaken, and Becky Saunders, from the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is that the site that was close to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't know where Vukovar is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that the site that Clyde Snow originally discovered in 1993 or so and they had to cover the skulls back up?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Vukovar is the site that Clyde Snow discovered; Brcko, I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Then it's my understanding that while you are in Bosnia again in the year 2000 to look at Lazete 1, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All of a sudden it came to someone's attention, your attention or who's attention, that there was a problem with what had been called Lazete 2 site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, I was told that the -- since we had time that they wanted me to re-excavate Lazete 2 because there was rumour that somebody had -- had been left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And if somebody -- you mean some bodies?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Some bodies, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine. Who would have left those bodies there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: It would have had to have been the ICTY PHR exhumation team during the 1996 exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell this Trial Chamber who was the coordinator and the head forensic archaeologist for that team?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Dr. Bill Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be a fair statement that you inherited this mess of Lazete 2 that Bill Haglund had created in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I would put it that way, but I would definitely say that I had to -- during the re-excavation of site, it was noted that the site was a lot larger than originally thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, have you, doctor, since then, and since your excavation of Lazete 2, and we're going to call it 2C, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever had a chance to speak directly with Dr. Haglund about this site?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We spoke briefly in Seattle, but not specifically. He just knew that I had to go back in there and he just said there was security issues, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He just said there were security issues and that's it?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, yeah, it wasn't something that I was going discuss with him in detail because I knew that -- I mean I had to write a report sooner or later so I just wanted him to know that I had been ordered to -- or asked to investigate Lazete 2 site, and, as of professional courtesy, I wanted him to know that it was me that was doing it, it was I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Doctor, would it be it fair statement that when you did speak with him briefly in Seattle and it was something that you did not want to discuss in detail with him, it was because it was sort of -- it was more than sort of -- but it was actually an embarrassment for Mr. Haglund to have left this site in the condition that he did, as a professional?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You'll have to ask him, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will, but I'm now asking you because you are an expert witness, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: There are circumstances where you can excavate graves partially. I mean, as you mentioned, if there were security issues, that might be one of them. You're not supposed to risk a living person to recover dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other issues that might have complicated Mr. Haglund's excavation of this site back in 1998 besides security? I'm not speaking -- I'm not asking you that from the grounds of what he told you, but what others told you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I was not part of any of the excavations before 1997, and no one has ever told me anything else, other than during that -- the 2000 year, they said that there was somebody that mentioned that there were some bodies left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your testimony earlier today you mentioned chain of custody, correct, of items?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Chain of custody is very important in your work, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And the way I understand your analysis on Lazete 2, there had been left there, by the team headed by Mr. Haglund over 500 and some pieces of evidence, excluding body parts, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry, 830 isolated artefacts recovered from the grave?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, from the surface and around the grave area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Some of those you would agree with me, could have helped to determine the identity of the bodies, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Mostly they were show cases. Most of the evidence we found, we found within the grave. I would have to look specifically if there were any artefacts that would help in the identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can appreciate that. But, for example, you found eight wristwatches, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And those wrist watches, had they been found in 1998, could have helped identify those bodies and helped the family members and loved ones of the deceased to know what happened or at least know where their loved ones were, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, personal belongings can help to give us a hypothesis for identification, but usually an identification would not be made just on personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But is it true, sir, that in the former Yugoslavia that there weren't a lot of dental records, for example; there weren't a lot of medical charts, for example; there weren't a lot of DNA samples that you could use, for example; and that this wasn't a characteristic site in that aspect?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it true that in the former Yugoslavia when you're excavating these graves from 1998 onwards, that even if you found, for example, a skull that had a full set of teeth, it likely there was no dental records to connect that skull with a certain person?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So in those sort of circumstances then it became more important to get the artefacts that -- that the clothing, the people wore, any IDs they might have had on them, any wristwatches they might have had on them, what kind of shoes they were wearing, so their last -- relatives could say, I think it might be my father or my son because he was wearing a certain kind of watch, for example.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you ever, sir, as -- in your field, in the line of work you've done in the last 12 or 13 years, would you ever discard certain items such as those?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And why wouldn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Because they're considered evidence and they could also, like you said, contribute to the identification of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And sir, in your 12 to 13 years of doing this type of work, can you tell me what you believe to be proper or improper about having two sites open at one time?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: It depends, if you have enough team members they can do different tasks. It's very proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And would that not include the proximity of the two sites to each other, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the proximity of the two sites to each other would definitely help in being able to conduct both simultaneously for a short amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your Lazete 2 report you have summary findings, then you go to exhumation procedures under paragraph 5, page 6, of your 26-page report, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You say, "the following general exhumation procedures were written by Richard Wright as a guideline for the excavation and exhumation of bodies, body parts, and artefactual evidence during ICTY exhumations." Did you not write that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me when, to your knowledge, Dr. Wright came up with these guidelines?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Must have been 1997.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, the first excavation we worked together on was Brcko, so it must have been during 1997. What we did is, we took the initial body and then tried to tailor it to each one of the -- of the different investigations, and this would be the protocol that we would give all of the team members that were working on the specific site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, real quickly, just to go back, since you're on that page, the one right before it, page 5, you have the people that worked underneath you, correct? Archaeologists and anthropologists, you have 11 of them?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Scene of crime officers, you have three?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you have one photographer?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And yourself, correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct. As well as a logistics team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: UN security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as UN security, actually people helping you out with the exhumation, removal of bodies, evidence, collection of evidence?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The demining team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Although they didn't help out with the grave; they demined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: They should be on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever had the opportunity to read Bill Haglund's report from the four exhumations he did in or around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how many people he had working for him, underneath him, being supervised by him, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question? I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to how many people that Mr. Haglund supervising him -- or he was supervising during his exhumations?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. No idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, go back real quick. You personally, have you ever worked or had two sites open simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In Guatemala, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And more than two?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And how far apart were they?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: They can -- well, several hundred kilometres sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And that's with the organisation -- the organisation in Guatemala that you are involved with heavily; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That's right, the Guatemala Forensic Anthropologists Foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And through that foundation, you worked with Dr. Clyde Snow from America quite often in South America, have you not?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In Central America, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In Central America. I'm about finished with this examination, doctor, and I appreciate your patience. I would like to just to go back to your report on Lazete 1, where you stated, my colleague asked you towards the end of her examination, it would be page 15, P02459.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Where you say that you -- "I estimate that a potential 68 bodies could have been removed during the robbing event."

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I know she asked you a little bit about that. I'm just going to ask you straight out: Isn't that really just speculation on your part because there was a lot of years in between?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Looking at the body layout of Lazete 1, it was clear that there was missing bodies. The other body groupings all were consistent, and therefore I make this estimation, believing that the same consistency of bodies and the same depth, group of bodies were present in the entire grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And that again is a guess or speculation based on other factors?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I think it's statement based on experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And speculation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. One last question. In all the time that you worked and you filed reports in Central America and the former Yugoslavia and all over the word, have you ever -- or would you ever allow a defence attorney to assist you in determining along with a pathologist the manner or cause of death?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. In all the time that you have worked in this field all over the world, including the former Yugoslavia, would you ever allow a criminal defence lawyer to assist you in determining the cause and manner of death? When I say you, you mean you and obviously the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I think that something that the experts have to determine. Not -- not the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. I have Madam Fauveau for Miletic, and then Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it right that the soil residues or other material found in the bodies or on the clothes can indicate the place where the victim was killed or where it was prior to death?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: It can, only if that material or soil is individualised enough and different from the area where it's found.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you worked on these sites, did you try to individualise that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, these were primary sites, and parts of the grave were taken away, not brought there. So it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it therefore fair to say that you cannot or you could not establish where the victims, the bodies, whose bodies you found, where they were killed?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Umm, we did not attempt to establish that. What we found was a large amount of ballistic evidence on the surface and within the grave. And then a grave with 127 bodies plus two bodies in a ditch.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to clarify a couple of questions and answers that you gave to Ms. Condon. Despite the fact that you are eminently capable of acting as an anthropologist, during the 2000 exhumations that you carried out, you weren't in fact required to act as an anthropologist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I was not asked to do any laboratory or morgue work. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do I take it from the fact that you were given written directions or you have penned the written directions how to conduct this exhumation by Richard Wright that he, in fact, was not there during the 2000 season either?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: He was not there during the time I was there. We only had a couple of days where we saw each other, and he basically handed over the team to me, and then I handed it back to him. But he was there -- the rest of the time he was there. Prior and after my -- my presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether there was, in fact, any anthropologists attached to this exhumation or these exhumations that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Anthropologists? Yes. There was several. Gordan Martin, Claudia Rivera, Mercedes Salalo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were they people who went to the morgue and carried out the sort of tasks that you might have carried out yourself, if you had been asked to?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, no, they were part of the field team. Who was on the morgue team, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So far as you are aware, therefore, not only did you not carry out any exercises to age the skeletons or the body parts, nobody else did either?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Umm, not from the excavation recovery team, but I'm sure they did it in the morgue, in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about determining the sex of the bodies? You didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, we did not determine the sex of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware of whether anybody else did that at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, Dr. John Clark was in charge of the morgue, if I'm not mistaken. I think I mention it in my report and of course they had a team there doing all -- individualising forensic anthropology traits, sex, age, stature and so forth, trauma analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as far as the calculation of the number of bodies that you recovered were concerned, you simply relied on the number of virtually complete bodies that you removed from the grave, that's 127 inside and two on the outside, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In Lazete 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I apologise, I should have been more specific, yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct. 129 bodies that required a body sheet to be filled out, plus body parts. I don't know the minimum number of individuals that was reached in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There were, in fact, only nine parts of bodies, weren't there, if you look at page 16 of your report?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Page 16. I don't think that's the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have page 16 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Nine, that's correct. Nine body parts. Plus one of the things that is not mentioned there is that loose bones were put into body part bags and assigned a body part number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But so far as you were concerned the only information that appeared in your report was the number of 129 bodies that you recovered?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could just have a look at e-court -- on e-court, please, at P02477, page 7. I hope somebody is going to blow that up so you can see it, Mr. Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, it's kind of small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What you knew as Lazete 2 has come to be known as Orahovac. You can see it, it's about six or seven down from the top.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I appreciate that you say you have never involved yourself in an MNI calculation, but as far as you were concerned the only figure you provided anybody with was 129, and yet we see there 131?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm finished with that on e-court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One last thing. There was, of course, a humanitarian aspect to this. Were you aware whether either at site or at the morgue DNA samples were being taken from the remains that you were recovering?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the morgue, because I wasn't there, but at the site there was no DNA samples being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Elderkin, do you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Peccerelli, we've come to the end of your testimony. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for having come over, and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, are there any documents you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. From what we can -- from what we can see there are no documents to be tendered with this witness. Tomorrow we will continue in the afternoon. Can I have a -- yeah, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't want to be the spoke in the wheel, but has Lazete 1 been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may have confused things. I understand -- well, Lazete 1 has been put in as Mr. Peccerelli's expert report under 94. And that is the only one of the reports we ask to be admitted. My understanding was that since it was his expert report and has been -- has been put in under 94 for some time, that it was already in evidence. But if I need to ask to the -- Lazete 1 to be tendered, I would do so. And his CV as well for Mr. Peccerelli, which -- the P numbers. I can give you the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think -- yes, Mr. Bourgon. I think -- I think, to try and streamline the procedure as must have as we can, there can be a question as to whether that was sufficient, because in reality we have never admitted it. So we are admitting it now. And when it's convenient, when you are in a position to tender Lazete 2, we'll consider, we'll consider the situation, because we haven't got it. We haven't even got a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. President, for Mr. Peccerelli's CV to be admitted, which is P02460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection. So that is admitted too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: For the record I should give you the P number for Lazete 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. I think the Registrar has it. Thank you. All right. We stand adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you so much, and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
